target: AG1’s claim that a national-holiday Election Day would remove voting barriers for low-income workers by giving them paid time off
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to provide paid time off, and many low-income workers are in private retail and service jobs with rigid schedules. Therefore, making Election Day a national holiday would not reliably give those workers paid time to vote and could still leave them with the same work-schedule barriers.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday is a strong turnout solution
objection: Research on voting reforms suggests that an Election Day holiday by itself is not especially effective at increasing turnout compared with other voting-access reforms. So the holiday alone is unlikely to produce the turnout gains supporters claim.

target: AG1’s implication that a national holiday is the best or sufficient reform for improving access
objection: More reliable alternatives exist, including state laws that require or encourage employer time off to vote and policies like automatic voter registration. Those reforms are presented as better tools than a holiday for improving voting access.

target: AG2’s claim that a national holiday would disadvantage low-income workers because they would still have to work
objection: On federal holidays many schools close and many workplaces reduce hours or close, and many low-income workers are in sectors that follow those scheduling reductions. So a holiday would make Election Day less like a normal work or school day and would reduce, rather than preserve, the scheduling barriers faced by low-income workers.

target: AG2’s argument that a holiday is ineffective because better reforms exist
objection: Even if a holiday alone is not sufficient, that does not mean it should be rejected. Voting-leave laws and automatic voter registration can be pursued alongside an Election Day holiday, so the existence of other reforms does not undercut the case for also making Election Day a holiday.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday-based election timing is not workable or effective
objection: Because 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, holiday or weekend election timing is portrayed as a widely used and administratively workable model. That international practice is offered as evidence against the claim that a holiday-based election day is impractical.

target: AG2’s claim that an Election Day holiday would not meaningfully improve turnout because work/school barriers would remain
objection: A holiday would remove the need to schedule around school and work on Election Day itself, so it would directly reduce the scheduling barrier that keeps many people from voting. The rebuttal argues that this day-of availability change is a real access improvement, not merely symbolic.

target: AG2’s claim that automatic voter registration is the relevant reform because the real barriers are pre-Election Day registration problems
objection: Even if some voters face pre-Election Day administrative hurdles, many people are blocked primarily by being unable to be free during the voting window. A national holiday addresses that day-of scheduling barrier, so it can still improve access even though it does not fix registration problems.

target: AG2’s argument that a holiday is not effective because people could instead use early voting or absentee voting
objection: The transcript argues that a holiday would increase national attention and encourage more voters to plan participation during the election period, including using advance voting options. So the holiday is framed as complementing early and absentee voting, not being negated by their existence.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday does not guarantee paid time off and therefore cannot help many workers
objection: The rebuttal says the key issue is reduced need to be at school or work during voting hours, not whether every worker is guaranteed paid leave. Even without a legal paid-time-off guarantee, a holiday would still lower practical scheduling barriers for many voters.

target: AG2’s argument that holiday election timing is unreliable because paid leave is not mandated for private employers
objection: The response assumes that what matters is whether schools and workplaces operate non-normally on the holiday. Since many schools close and many workplaces reduce hours or close on holidays, the policy is said to reduce scheduling conflict even without a statutory paid-leave requirement.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would disadvantage low-income workers
objection: The rebuttal contends that low-income workers are harmed by rigid schedules and lack of availability during voting hours, so a national holiday that reduces school/work obligations would help rather than hurt them. It rejects the idea that the holiday would chiefly create unpaid-leave problems.

target: AG1’s broader claim that a holiday solves the main access problem
objection: Turnout barriers are not only day-of scheduling issues; they also include pre-Election Day administrative and eligibility hurdles such as registration and keeping registration current. A national holiday does not fix those problems, so it cannot substitute for reforms that directly address them.

target: AG1’s appeal to automatic voter registration as a separate, optional reform that does not weaken the holiday proposal
objection: Automatic voter registration directly targets pre-Election Day eligibility and administrative barriers, whereas an Election Day holiday mainly changes day-of scheduling. Because those are different kinds of barriers, the holiday cannot do the job of automatic voter registration.
